chapters.title: Chapter 2: Market Impact and Liquidity: Why Big Money Moves Prices

lessons.title: Order Book Depth and Bid-Ask Spread on the NSE

children.text: Chapter 1 talked about market impact and liquidity informally, as things that grow with order size. To make any of that precise, this chapter starts from the object where impact and liquidity actually live: the order book. Before capacity math means anything, you need to be fluent in two basics every desk assumes you already know, bid-ask spread and order book depth.
What an Order Book Actually Shows You

Every NSE-listed stock trades against a live limit order book: a running list of buy orders (bids) and sell orders (asks), each sitting at a specific price with a specific quantity, ranked by price and then by the time the order arrived. Trading terminals such as Zerodha's Kite typically show five levels of this book on each side, often labeled Best 5. The best bid and best ask, the top of the book, are what you see quoted as the current price. Everything else in the book is quantity waiting behind that price.

children.text: Bid-Ask Spread: The First, Smallest Cost of Trading

markDefs.definition: The gap between the best bid (highest price a buyer is willing to pay) and the best ask (lowest price a seller is willing to accept). Buying at the ask and immediately selling at the bid loses you exactly this amount.

children.text: The gap between the best bid and the best ask is called the

, and it is the smallest, most unavoidable cost of trading a liquid instrument: buy at the ask, sell at the bid, and you have already paid the spread before the stock has moved a single rupee in your favor. In the order book above, the spread is Rs 0.10 on a stock trading near Rs 248.55, about 0.04 percent, typical of a reasonably liquid NSE mid-cap.

stats.label: Large-cap NSE stock
stats.context: Often just a single tick wide

stats.label: Liquid mid-cap stock
stats.context: Still a minor cost relative to brokerage and STT

stats.label: Thinly traded small or micro-cap
stats.context: Can outweigh brokerage and STT combined

children.text: Depth: Why the Best Price Isn't the Whole Story

markDefs.definition: The quantity available to trade at each price level in the order book, on both the bid and ask sides. Deep books can absorb large orders near the current price; thin books cannot.

children.text: The best ask in the table above is only good for 400 shares. That is a question of

. Try to buy more than 400 shares with a plain market order and the exchange fills the remainder at the next best price, then the next, a process traders call walking the book. The further you have to walk, the worse your average execution price gets relative to the price you saw quoted before you clicked buy. This is market impact in its rawest, most mechanical form, before you even reach the more formal models in the next lesson.

body.caption: The weighted average execution price when an order is large enough to walk through multiple levels of the book, where q_i and p_i are the quantity filled and price at each level.

body.title: Walking the Book
body.prompt: Using the order book table above, you place a market order to buy 1,500 shares. Filling it takes all 400 shares at Rs 248.60, all 650 shares at Rs 248.65, and the remaining 450 shares at Rs 248.70. What is your weighted average purchase price per share, in rupees, rounded to two decimals?
body.explanation: Cost = (400 x 248.60) + (650 x 248.65) + (450 x 248.70) = 99,440 + 161,622.50 + 111,915 = 372,977.50. Divide by 1,500 shares to get Rs 248.65 per share, about half a rupee worse than the Rs 248.60 you would have paid if the entire order had filled at the best ask alone.

children.text: Market Orders vs Limit Orders: Certainty vs Price Control

A market order takes whatever liquidity is sitting in the book, walking through levels if needed, in exchange for near-certain, immediate execution. A limit order instead sits in the book at a price you choose, adding to the depth on your side, and only executes if someone else is willing to trade at that price. The tradeoff is the same one that runs through this entire course: certainty of execution against control over price.

columns.label: Market Order
points: Executes immediately, assuming any liquidity exists at all
Price is whatever the book gives you, including walking through multiple levels for a large order
Takes liquidity from the book rather than adding to it
Right tool when certainty of execution matters more than price

columns.label: Limit Order
points: Guarantees no fill worse than your specified price
May not execute at all if the market never reaches your limit
Adds liquidity to the book while it waits in the queue
Right tool when price control matters more than immediate certainty

body.text: A large market order in a thinly traded small-cap is one of the fastest ways to hand your own edge to the order book. Before placing size in any stock, check the depth. If your intended quantity is bigger than what sits at the first one or two price levels, either break the order into smaller pieces or switch to a limit order and be patient. Chapter 6 covers dedicated execution algorithms built exactly for this problem.

Every price you see quoted is only a promise for a limited quantity. The moment your order is bigger than that quantity, you are no longer trading at the price on the screen, you are trading against the depth behind it.

points: An order book ranks bids and asks by price and then by time, and only the top of the book, the best bid and best ask, is what you see quoted as the current price.
Bid-ask spread is the smallest, most unavoidable cost of trading, widening sharply as you move from large-caps to thinly traded small and micro-caps.
Depth determines how much quantity is available before your order has to walk to worse prices, and walking the book is market impact in its most mechanical, visible form.

Market orders trade certainty of execution for price control, limit orders trade price control for certainty of execution, and every execution decision in this course is some version of that same tradeoff.
